prohibited_recommendations: Do not give corticosteroids as monotherapy.
Do not attribute neuropathy to spinal anaesthesia without consideration of timing (3+ weeks post-op argues against direct injury).
required_recommendations: Monitor respiratory function and autonomic stability closely.
Lactation-safe medication review; IVIG and PLEX are compatible with breastfeeding.

avoided_actions.rationale: GBS is a peripheral nerve / nerve-root disorder; EEG has no role in diagnosis unless atypical CNS features (encephalopathy, seizures) are present.
Echocardiography is not indicated in typical GBS; reserve for pre-existing cardiac disease or unexplained hemodynamic instability after autonomic causes are excluded.
Head CT contributes no diagnostic information in GBS; the disease is peripheral and CT does not visualise nerve roots reliably.
Brain MRI is reserved for atypical features (encephalopathy, CNS signs, transverse myelitis on differential). In classic GBS it does not aid diagnosis.

accepted: Guillain-Barré syndrome, AMSAN variant (post-partum / post-cesarean trigger)

differential.diagnosis: Spinal anaesthesia-related neuropathy / cauda equina injury
differential.key_features: Anatomically restricted (one or two nerve roots) and asymmetric — pattern here is symmetric bilateral ascending, inconsistent with anaesthetic injury.
Pregnancy and the post-partum period are recognised triggers for autoimmune polyneuropathies; differentiated longitudinally.
Subacute and length-dependent; areflexia possible but no acute progression with elevated CSF protein.
Asymmetric mononeuropathy multiplex; symmetric ascending pattern argues against.
Patient was discharged from uncomplicated post-op and represented at home.

key_clinical_evidence: AMSAN variant: symmetric motor + sensory axonal involvement on EMG with low CMAP and SNAP amplitudes.
Pregnancy and post-partum period are recognised immune-trigger windows; do not require an additional infectious antecedent.
Spinal anaesthesia-related neuropathy is anatomically restricted and asymmetric; the symmetric ascending presentation does not fit.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Anaesthetic injuries are anatomically restricted and present within days, not 3+ weeks; the symmetric ascending GBS pattern is inconsistent with that mechanism.
red_herrings.data_point: Recent spinal anaesthesia 22 days before presentation
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on a direct anaesthetic injury rather than an autoimmune polyneuropathy.

sequence_constraints.reason: Document respiratory status (FVC/NIF) before committing to IVIG vs plasma exchange — severe respiratory compromise mandates ICU triage and may influence treatment choice and timing.
Renal function, IgA screen, and CBC must be reviewed before IVIG to mitigate renal failure, anaphylaxis (IgA-deficient patients), and aseptic meningitis risk.

specialized_test.impression: This is an ABNORMAL nerve conduction study. 1. Severely prolonged distal motor latencies and severely reduced conduction velocities in bilateral posterior tibial and peroneal motor nerves, with markedly reduced CMAP amplitudes (0.8–1.2 mV); upper extremity motor NCS borderline normal. 2. Absent sural sensory nerve action potentials bilaterally; reduced median sensory amplitudes (8 µV). 3. Absent F-waves bilaterally (posterior tibial, peroneal). 4. Absent H-reflex bilaterally. Severely reduced CMAP amplitudes in lower extremity motor nerves with absent sensory responses — predominantly axonal pattern with lower extremity predominance

quantitative_data.pattern: Generalized severe sensorimotor axonal neuropathy predominant in lower extremities — acute motor-sensory axonal (AMSAN) electrodiagnostic pattern

patient.chief_complaint: Progressive bilateral leg weakness over 2 weeks, unable to walk, 22 days after emergency cesarean section under spinal anesthesia.

past_medical_history: G1P1 — emergency cesarean section 22 days ago (38 weeks, fetal distress)

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. P. is a 29-year-old primiparous woman presenting 22 days after an emergency lower-segment cesarean section performed under spinal anesthesia at 38 weeks for fetal distress. She was discharged on postoperative day 5 with mild bilateral lower limb numbness and tingling, which was attributed to residual effects of spinal anesthesia. However, starting approximately 8 days after surgery, she began noticing progressive bilateral leg weakness that was insidious in onset. The weakness progressed from distal to proximal over the following two weeks. She could initially perform daily activities with assistance, but is now completely unable to stand or support herself. She reports burning and tingling in both lower extremities extending to mid-thigh. She denies any upper limb weakness. There is no bowel or bladder dysfunction. She denies dysphagia, dysarthria, diplopia, or visual changes. There was no preceding respiratory illness or diarrheal illness identified. There is no prior history of neuropathy or neurological disease. She is concerned about her ability to care for her newborn. Given the recent spinal anesthesia and surgery, the presentation raised concern for a post-surgical complication such as epidural hematoma or lumbar epidural abscess, though she has no fever, back pain, or bladder dysfunction.
